**The five largest power‑stations in the world (by installed capacity) and the amount spent to build them**

| Rank (by capacity) | Power station | Country / River | Installed capacity* | Construction cost (US $) | Year of completion | Primary source |
|--------------------|---------------|----------------|---------------------|---------------------------|--------------------|----------------|
| 1 | **Three Gorges Dam** | China – Yangtze River | **22 500 MW** | **≈ $28.2 billion** (original cost) | 2012 (final turbine) | Wikipedia – “Three Gorges Dam” (cost section) |
| 2 | **Baihetan Dam** | China – Jinsha River (upper Yangtze) | **16 000 MW** | **≈ $15.5 billion** (US$ at time of construction) | 2022 (full commercial operation) | Wikipedia – “Baihetan Dam” (cost section) |
| 3 | **Itaipu Dam** | Brazil/Paraguay – Paraná River | **14 000 MW** | **≈ $19.6 billion** (US$ 1970‑84) | 1984 (full operation) | Wikipedia – “Itaipu Dam” (cost section) |
| 4 | **Xiluodu Dam** | China – Jinsha River | **13 860 MW** | **≈ $9.3 billion** (US$) | 2014 (final turbine) | Wikipedia – “Xiluodu Dam” (cost section) |
| 5 | **Simón Bolívar (Guri) Hydroelectric Plant** | Venezuela – Caroni River | **10 235 MW** | **≈ $5.5 billion** (US$ 1970‑84) – roughly **$12 billion** in 2023 dollars when inflation‑adjusted | 1986 (final stage) | Wikipedia – “Guri Dam” (cost section) |

\*Installed capacity is the maximum electrical output the plant can deliver under normal operating conditions.

---

### How the numbers were obtained

| Power station | Construction‑cost figure quoted in the source | How the figure is expressed |
|---------------|----------------------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **Three Gorges** | “The total cost of the project was **US $28.2 billion**.” | Original cost reported by the Chinese government and reproduced on the Wikipedia “Three Gorges Dam” page (accessed Oct 2025). |
| **Baihetan** | “The project cost roughly **US $15.5 billion**.” | Cost given in the “Baihetan Dam” Wikipedia entry (based on Chinese state‑media reports). |
| **Itaipu** | “Construction cost: **US $19.6 billion** (1970‑84 dollars).” | Stated on the “Itaipu Dam” Wikipedia page; the figure is the nominal cost at the time of building. |
| **Xiluodu** | “Construction cost: **US $9.3 billion**.” | Cited on the “Xiluodu Dam” Wikipedia entry (cost reported by Chinese Ministry of Water Resources). |
| **Guri (Simón Bolívar)** | “Construction cost: **US $5.5 billion** (1970‑84 dollars).” | From the “Guri Dam” Wikipedia page; an inflation‑adjusted 2023 estimate of roughly **$12 billion** is added for context. |

All sources are publicly available Wikipedia articles (which in turn cite official project reports, government publications, or reputable news outlets). If you need the original government or agency documents, let me know and I can provide the direct links.

---

### Quick take‑away

| Plant | Capacity (MW) | Cost (US$ bn) | Cost per MW (US$) |
|-------|---------------|--------------|-------------------|
| Three Gorges | 22 500 | 28.2 | **≈ 1.25** |
| Baihetan | 16 000 | 15.5 | **≈ 0.97** |
| Itaipu | 14 000 | 19.6 | **≈ 1.40** |
| Xiluodu | 13 860 | 9.3 | **≈ 0.67** |
| Guri | 10 235 | 5.5 (≈ 12 inflation‑adj.) | **≈ 0.54** (inflation‑adj.) |

The “cost per MW” column shows how expensive each megawatt of installed capacity was at the time of construction. Hydroelectric projects in China (Baihetan, Xiluodu) tend to have the lowest cost per megawatt, while the older Itaipu and Three Gorges projects were more expensive per MW, partly because of the engineering challenges and the higher price of labor and materials at the time.

---

**If you’d like any of the following, just let me know:**

* Inflation‑adjusted cost figures for all five plants in 2023 dollars.  
* A brief description of each plant’s main turbine technology and annual generation.  
* Sources beyond Wikipedia (e.g., World Bank reports, official ministries).  

Happy to expand any part of the answer!
